newsitem.title: IRAQ: U.S. sponsored Kurds prepare to flee N.Iraq.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sponsored Kurds prepare to flee N.Iraq.

text.p: Hundreds of Kurds working for U.S. aid and military groups hid in fear on Friday and prepared for evacuation from Iraq, their departure marking the demise of U.S. influence in country's rebel north.
"At midnight last night the Americans in Silopi gave the go ahead for the evacuation," said a Kurd working for the major U.S. government agency, the Office of Foreign Disaster Assistance (OFDA).

"They said to contact the governor of Dohuk to work out the details and explian the plan. He said he would provide security and transportation to the border," the Kurd, who did not wish to be identified for fear of repurcussions, told Reuters.

Staff at the northern Iraqi centre of a U.S.-led force shielding Kurds from Baghdad moved to the Turkish border town of Silopi as a Kurdish militia, backed by President Saddam Hussein, began an assault on August 31 to take control the whole region.

OFDA workers said people employed by the organisation -- a total of 640 people -- would be the first to be evacuated. The large portion of the total evacuees were expected to be workers for OFDA or its many affiliates.

At least 120 OFDA workers and their families hid in hotels or private residences in Dohuk, packed 15 or 20 to a house. Their relatives, from all over northern Iraq, crammed into the houses, visiting for perhaps the last time.

In Zakho town near the Turkish border around 100 Kurds who had worked for aid groups and the U.S. military were holed up in a U.S.-controlled compound, hoping to be escorted across to Silopi. Outside the compound Kurdish peshmerga fighters stood guard with machineguns. A red, white and blue logo signifying their U.S. sponsors had been sewn on to their uniforms.
Those to be evacuated include administrators, drivers, guards, programme officers and messangers for U.S. groups. Most are likely Kurds, with some Arabs and maybe Turkomans.

"Yesterday we received a fax from Washington asking for the names of all those NGOs (non-governmental organisations) with grants from OFDA and names of their local and foreign staff," said another Kurd who worked for OFDA.
He said the plan was being worked out by the evacuees and the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), which controls northern Iraq after its Baghdad-backed push against a rival faction.

It was unclear exactly when the evacuees would leave. No one appeared to have been evacuated by Friday afternoon. They are expected to leave in a convoy of buses at least to Zakho and then maybe airlifted out or picked up by cars or buses.
They are then expected to remain for up to three months in Silopi before settling in the United States.
The refugees said they were worried that Saddam's forces would attack them as they tried to leave.
The most afraid are the ones from Arbil, the main Kurdish city that the KDP and Saddam's forces captured last month.
KDP officials say the evacuation is unnecessary and that the U.S. will lose valuable influence in the region by this.
"You can see the situation here is okay. We haven't any agreement with Iraq and we are about to form a local government," said Abdul Aziz, the KDP chief for the Zakho area.

"So why at this time is the American government advising local employees to leave?," he said. The KDP asked for the allied military staff to return to Zakho and for the NGOs to return to the region, saying the Kurds still needed aid.
Washington launched cruise missile attacks against Iraqi targets in the south in retaliation for Saddam's involvement in the fighting. In the north, it has so far done nothing.
"If they have advised everyone to leave, believe me, America will lose a lot of interest and control in northern Iraq," a KDP official said. "Their influence will be damaged here."
